newsitem.title: DUBAI: Relatives of India crash victims ask about bodies.
newsitem.headline: Relatives of India crash victims ask about bodies.

text.p: Relatives of the Saudi victims of the world's worst mid-air collision have been calling Jeddah airport all day to ask a painful question -- when will the remains of their loved ones be sent home from India?
"The brother and family of the captain, Khalid al-Shubaily, have been calling all the time to ask when his remains would be returned," a Jeddah airport official told Reuters.

Al-Shubaily, a veteran pilot with more than 20 years flying experience, was the captain of the Saudi Arabian Airlines Boeing 747 which collided with a Kazakh Ilyushin IL-76 freighter near New Delhi on Tuesday.
"Relatives of the crew members had come to the airport but have left. Now they just want to find out when the bodies will be coming back," said the official who declined to be named.

There was no immediate explanation for the disaster, which killed some 350 people, but speculation ran from inadequate equipment at Delhi airport to pilot misunderstanding of ground controller instructions.

Authorities at a special emergency centre at King Abdul Aziz Internationl Airport in Jeddah spent the day scrambling for details on the passengers and fielding questions from distraught relatives, the official said.

It is still not clear when the remains of the victims would be flown home to the desert kingdom and details of the passengers on Saudi Arabian Airlines flight SV 763 were being faxed to Jeddah airport from India on Wednesday night.
It was bound for Dhahran and Jeddah.
"We are expecting the bodies to be sent home and we are waiting," said the official.
Relatives of 27-year-old Khalid Baakeel, a Saudi steward who served at Saudi Arabian Airlines for seven years, first learned of the disaster on television.

"First we heard about it on television. Then the airlines called us and tried to break it to us gently. They didn't want to hurt us," his older brother, who requested anonymity, told Reuters by telephone from Jeddah.
"But when we figured out what flight he was on and realised that that plane had crashed, we knew it was true. He is dead," he added.

The airport official said there were a total of 312 people on board the Saudi jumbo. They were mostly workers from India and Nepal and included some Europeans and one Saudi passenger, he said without elaborating.
A Saudi newspaper said the victims included 215 Indians, nine Nepalese and three Pakistanis.
Two as yet unidentified American women were on the flight along with Englishwoman Karen McCoy, who was returning to her job in Saudi Arabia from a holiday in India.
Of the 23 crew members who included a Jordanian, 11 were Saudi, including six undercover security men to prevent hijackings, the official said.
One crew member was 31-year-old Jameel Baabdullah, who is survived by three young children, two daughters and a son.
"We don't know what is happening now," said his brother Ahmed from Jeddah by telephone. "We are just waiting for the body."
Saudi television on Wednesday showed footage of the crash site but the disaster was not given a high profile on news programmes.
